title: The Patomskiy Crater: Siberia's 1,000,000-Ton Mystery (1949)
description:
Deep within the remote Patom Highlands of southeastern Siberia sits a massive, ring-shaped mound of shattered limestone weighing an estimated one million tons. First described by Russian geologist Vadim Kolpakov in 1949, this giant formation has challenged scientists for over seven decades.

We examine the full timeline of the Patomskiy crater, from early hypotheses of ultra-dense meteorite strikes and the Tunguska impact to modern geophysical surveys revealing deep-earth volcanic breakthroughs. Explore how tree-ring analysis and gravimetric studies at the 2010 Saint Petersburg conference reshaped our understanding of this Siberian anomaly.

What force do you believe pushed nearly nine million cubic feet of rock out of the earth three hundred years ago? Leave your thoughts in the comments.
look: 1949 to present, remote Siberian taiga, Patom Highlands, rugged limestone, overcast mist, muted slate grey and deep green

The mystery of the Patomskiy crater remains unsolved.
What force do you believe pushed one million tons of rock out of the Siberian taiga?
short.narration: Deep in the Siberian taiga sits a one-million-ton mound of shattered limestone. Known as the Patomskiy crater, it stands forty meters high above the trees. Its base spans five hundred and twenty feet across the Patom Highlands. At the top, a ring-shaped crown cradles a central twelve-meter mound. Geologist Vadim Kolpakov first documented the massive structure in 1949. For decades, experts questioned what force could move such immense weight. One early hypothesis suggested an impact from an ultra-dense meteorite. Others wondered if it was a fragment of the Tunguska event. But researchers found no cosmogenic evidence in the crushed limestone blocks. Scientific interest shifted to subterranean forces deep beneath the crust. Dendrochronology established that the mound formed about three hundred years ago. At a 2010 conference, geologist Viktor Sergeyevich Antipin presented crucial findings. Morphological data and weathered breccias pointed toward an extrusive volcanic origin. Geophysical teams measured gravimetric data across the peculiar rock formation. They confirmed the mound resulted from intense endogenetic gas breakthroughs. Deep fluids and carbon monoxide gases had violently forced stone upward.
